title: Snowflake and Iceberg
summary: How Snowflake reads and writes Iceberg tables in your own storage, the difference between Snowflake-managed and externally managed tables, and when to choose Iceberg over native tables.

blocks.text: Native Snowflake tables (chapter 26) live in storage only Snowflake can read. Iceberg tables in Snowflake keep data and metadata in **your** bucket, in the open format from Part V, so other engines can use the same copy. The key design question is not 'Iceberg or not' but **which catalog owns each table's commits**.

head: Snowflake-managed
Externally managed
rows: Another catalog: Glue, a REST catalog such as Open Catalog/Polaris, or plain metadata files in object storage
The external engines; Snowflake mostly reads (write support through REST catalogs is evolving: check the current documentation)
Close to native tables: DML, clustering, time travel, governance policies
Read-oriented; metadata must be refreshed to see new snapshots
Read through a catalog that exposes Snowflake's metadata
Read and write through their catalog
Snowflake runs compaction and snapshot cleanup

blocks.text: Both kinds store Parquet data files and Iceberg metadata in a location you own, defined by an **external volume**.

An external volume is an account-level object that names a storage location and the cloud identity Snowflake uses to access it, much like a storage integration (chapter 27) but for Iceberg tables. You grant the Snowflake-generated principal access in your cloud account, typically read-write for managed tables and read-only for external ones.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table
blocks.text:
CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME lake_vol
  STORAGE_LOCATIONS = (
    ( NAME = 'lake-s3'
      STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
      STORAGE_BASE_URL = 's3://acme-lake/iceberg/'
      STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-iceberg' ) );

DESC EXTERNAL VOLUME lake_vol;   -- shows the IAM user and external id to trust

CREATE ICEBERG TABLE gold.daily_revenue (
    order_date DATE,
    region     STRING,
    revenue    NUMBER(18,2))
  CATALOG         = 'SNOWFLAKE'
  EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'lake_vol'
  BASE_LOCATION   = 'gold/daily_revenue';

Keep the external volume in the same cloud region as the Snowflake account. Cross-region access adds latency and egress charges on every query, and the bucket's lifecycle rules must never delete files Iceberg still references.

For tables owned elsewhere, a **catalog integration** tells Snowflake how to find their metadata: in AWS Glue, in an Iceberg REST catalog (Open Catalog, Polaris, Unity Catalog and others), or directly from a metadata file path in object storage. The Iceberg table in Snowflake then points at the remote table.

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: externally managed table (check current docs for all parameters)
blocks.text:
CREATE CATALOG INTEGRATION glue_int
  CATALOG_SOURCE    = GLUE
  TABLE_FORMAT      = ICEBERG
  CATALOG_NAMESPACE = 'sales'
  GLUE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-glue'
  GLUE_CATALOG_ID   = '123456789012'
  GLUE_REGION       = 'eu-west-1'
  ENABLED           = TRUE;

CREATE ICEBERG TABLE bronze.orders
  EXTERNAL_VOLUME    = 'lake_vol'
  CATALOG            = 'glue_int'
  CATALOG_TABLE_NAME = 'orders'
  AUTO_REFRESH       = TRUE;

Snowflake caches the remote table's current snapshot. **Auto-refresh** polls the catalog and picks up new snapshots; without it you run `ALTER ICEBERG TABLE ... REFRESH`. Either way there is a delay between an external commit and Snowflake seeing it, so freshness SLAs must include it.

Defining tables one by one does not scale to hundreds of tables. A **catalog-linked database** connects a Snowflake database to a remote REST catalog and discovers its namespaces and tables automatically, keeping them in sync. Capabilities, including writes back through the remote catalog, are evolving; check the current documentation.
28.4 Letting other engines read Snowflake-managed tables
A Snowflake-managed Iceberg table is valid Iceberg in your bucket, but other engines need a catalog to find its current metadata. Options at a conceptual level:

items: **Sync to Open Catalog**: configure Snowflake to publish managed tables to a Snowflake Open Catalog account (a catalog integration used for *catalog sync*). Spark, Trino or Flink then read through Open Catalog's REST endpoint with vended credentials. In Open Catalog these appear as external tables, so other engines cannot commit to them.

**Snowflake's own Iceberg REST endpoint**: Snowflake exposes catalog access for its managed Iceberg tables through its Horizon catalog for external engines; check the current documentation for the endpoint and supported operations.
**Direct metadata path**: point an engine at the latest metadata file. Fine for tests, fragile in production because the path changes on every commit.

blocks.title: Snowflake-managed tables shared out
blocks.caption: One writer (Snowflake), many readers through a REST catalog.

head: Choose
When
rows: Only Snowflake reads the data; you want every Snowflake feature, fail-safe and zero operational overhead; data is relatively small or highly governed inside Snowflake
Snowflake is the main writer, but Spark, ML platforms or other teams must read the same copy without exports; you want storage in your account
Another engine (Spark, Flink) owns ingestion or the lakehouse; Snowflake is one consumer among several

items: **Storage** for Iceberg tables is billed by your cloud provider, not Snowflake. There is no Snowflake fail-safe for them; protect the bucket with versioning or replication if you need recovery beyond snapshots.
**Compute** for queries is the same warehouse credits. Snowflake-managed tables also consume compute for automatic maintenance; for external tables you pay for maintenance in the owning engine.
**Performance** on well-maintained Iceberg tables is close to native for many workloads; badly maintained external tables (small files, many deletes) are slow in every engine, including Snowflake.
**Feature gaps** between native and Iceberg tables shrink with each release, but some still exist; check the current documentation before relying on a feature.

blocks.text: Do not let two writers own one table: for example Spark writing directly to the bucket path of a Snowflake-managed table. Snowflake would not see those files, and its maintenance may later delete them as orphans.

blocks.title: Shared customer 360
blocks.text: A retailer builds customer features in Snowflake with dbt and the data science platform trains models in Spark on the same data. The gold `customer_features` table is a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table synced to Open Catalog. Snowflake is the only writer; Spark reads through Open Catalog with vended credentials. The previous nightly 400 GB Parquet export, and the drift between the export and the warehouse, disappeared.

blocks.title: Place twelve tables
blocks.text: Your lakehouse has Flink writing bronze CDC tables to Iceberg in a Polaris catalog, Spark building silver, and Snowflake used by analysts and finance. Twelve gold tables are built in Snowflake with dbt; three of them are also used by a Spark ML pipeline. Decide for each layer and table group: native, Snowflake-managed Iceberg or externally managed Iceberg; which catalog owns commits; how Snowflake discovers external tables; and how freshness and maintenance work end to end.

items: Iceberg tables in Snowflake keep data and metadata in your bucket, defined by an external volume.
Snowflake-managed tables: Snowflake commits and maintains; others read through a catalog.
Externally managed tables: another catalog owns commits; Snowflake reads via a catalog integration and refreshes metadata.
Catalog-linked databases and catalog sync scale integration beyond single tables; their capabilities are evolving.
Native tables remain simplest when only Snowflake uses the data; Iceberg pays off when several engines share one copy.
Every table needs exactly one owning writer and one catalog of record.

blocks.q: A Glue-cataloged Iceberg table is updated by Spark. Snowflake queries it through a catalog integration. Why might Snowflake show slightly older data?
options: Snowflake reads its cached snapshot until auto-refresh or a manual REFRESH picks up the new metadata
Iceberg readers always lag by one snapshot
blocks.explain: Snowflake tracks the remote table's current snapshot and updates it on refresh. No copy is made; the delay is the refresh interval.

blocks.q: Who pays for the storage of a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table?
options: Snowflake bills it as regular table storage including fail-safe
It is billed by your cloud provider for your bucket
blocks.explain: Iceberg tables live in your external volume, so storage is on your cloud bill. Snowflake still bills compute, including maintenance of managed tables.

blocks.q: What is the role of an external volume?
options: It is a Snowflake-managed internal stage for Iceberg data
It is a catalog that other engines query
It defines the storage location and the cloud identity Snowflake uses to read and write Iceberg files
It caches remote Parquet files on warehouse SSDs
blocks.explain: The external volume is the storage side: where files go and how Snowflake authenticates. The catalog side is handled by Snowflake itself or a catalog integration.

blocks.q: Analysts only use Snowflake, the data is 300 GB, and governance requires the strongest built-in recovery options. Which table type fits best?
options: Snowflake-managed Iceberg synced to Open Catalog
A directory of Parquet files read as an external table
blocks.explain: With a single engine, Iceberg adds operational surface without benefit, and native tables include fail-safe. Iceberg pays off when other engines need the same copy.
